Set this beside the honest secular research on forgiveness, tested against Scripture, which consistently finds that harbored resentment corrodes the one who holds it, raising anxiety and hardening the body, while the release of a grievance measurably heals the one who lets it go. The finding gets the symptom right, that unforgiveness poisons its keeper, and cannot reach the root, because the psychological account can describe the benefit of letting go without supplying the ocean of divine mercy that alone makes the letting go possible. Then take the hardest pastoral turn, the difference between forgiveness and reconciliation, holding firmly that forgiveness is the release of the debt worked in the wounded for their freedom, while reconciliation requires the repentance of the offender and can be neither demanded nor rushed, and that where there is ongoing harm the call is to safety and not to a hollow absolution. The aim is to keep the petition both grace-grounded and serious, refusing the cheap reading that makes forgiveness a wage and the cheap reading that makes it optional, and to feel that the forgiven, precisely as the forgiven, forgive.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group carries a real and deep wound, a betrayal or an abuse from years back, and when the session turns to forgiveness she goes rigid and says, with quiet force, that she has been told her whole life she has to forgive, that people keep using this prayer to tell her to excuse what was done to her, and that she is tired of it. She is not being stubborn. She is protecting herself from a cruelty that has been done to her in God's name. Here is the work for the leader, and it must not repeat that cruelty. Do not press the petition on her. First, name plainly that she has been wronged twice, once by the offender and again by everyone who used forgiveness as a whip. Then, gently, offer her a different definition than the one she was handed, because the forgiveness Jesus teaches is not excusing the wrong, not forgetting it, not calling it acceptable, and never returning to the reach of someone still doing harm. It is the eventual release of her right to make the person pay, worked slowly by the Spirit for her own freedom, so the debt no longer owns her, and it does not require reconciliation with an unrepentant or dangerous person. Tell her there is no timeline she owes anyone. Where the wound is this deep, point her toward real help and toward safety, and make clear that the God of this prayer is on the side of the wounded, not the one who harmed her, and never asks her to call the wound acceptable in order to be free of it.

sessions.title: Lead Us Not Into Temptation, But Deliver Us From Evil
sessions.aim: To take seriously the last petition's request for protection in the testing, to name the reality of evil the prayer refuses to explain away, and to end where the prayer ends, on the doxology that hands the kingdom, the power, and the glory back to the God they always belonged to.
sessions.summary: Bell says the prayer does not end in triumph. It ends with a request for rescue, lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, a petition that assumes we are weaker than we think and the danger is more real than we admit. The real question begins with a puzzle the church has argued over for centuries, because James says plainly that God tempts no one, so why would we ask God not to lead us into temptation. The Greek word peirasmos means testing as much as temptation, and the petition is best heard as a plea, do not let the testing be more than we can bear, do not abandon us to the trial, spare us the hour we would not survive. Even Pope Francis, in 2019, approved a change to the wording in the Roman Catholic liturgy for exactly this reason, to make clear that God is not the author of our temptation. Bell takes the strong case of the modern skeptic, that evil is a primitive category, that what religion calls the evil one is really just psychology and circumstance, that grown-ups do not pray to be delivered from a devil. He grants what is true, that evil has been used as a lazy explanation and a tool of fear. But a world that has abolished the word evil has not abolished the thing, and the twentieth century, of all centuries, is a strange place to argue that the category is naive. Then the doxology, the ending that later manuscripts added and the church has prayed for nearly two thousand years, for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Then the reversal. The prayer that began by hallowing God's name ends by handing him everything, the kingdom we tried to keep, the power we thought was ours, the glory we kept taking. We end the prayer smaller than we started, and it turns out that is the only place a human being was ever safe.

keyScripture.why: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, the final petition that confesses our weakness in the testing and our need of rescue from a real evil, ending the prayer not in self-confidence but in dependence on the God who delivers.

discussion.q: Bell says the prayer does not end in triumph but in a request for rescue, assuming we are weaker than we think. What is it like to end the most important prayer with lead us not into temptation instead of with confidence?
discussion.behind: Open on the humility of the ending. We would have ended the prayer on victory, and Jesus ends it on a plea for protection. Help the room feel that this is not defeatism but honesty about the human condition, that the strongest thing we can do is admit we are not strong enough and ask to be kept. The ending is dependence, not triumph.

discussion.q: James says God tempts no one, so the church has heard this petition as a plea, do not let the testing be more than we can bear. Where have you needed God to spare you from a trial you knew you could not survive on your own?
discussion.behind: Draw out the lived meaning of the petition. Everyone has known a testing that felt beyond them, and the petition gives words for the fear. Help the room ask honestly to be spared, to be kept out of the hour they could not withstand, which is a legitimate and humble request, not a lack of faith. Handle the puzzle about God and temptation with the plain reading, God tests but does not entice to evil.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that evil is a primitive category, that grown-ups do not pray to be delivered from a devil. What is true in that suspicion, and why is the twentieth century a strange place to argue evil is naive?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves for the skeptic in the room. The suspicion is fair, evil has been used lazily and as a tool of fear, and the church has cried devil when the real problem was its own sin. Grant it. Then press the honest counter, that a century of industrialized murder makes the confident abolition of the word evil look less like maturity and more like amnesia. Let the skeptic feel understood before the turn.

discussion.q: The prayer ends by handing God the kingdom, the power, and the glory, the very three things we spend our lives trying to keep. Which of the three do you hold onto hardest, and what would it mean to hand it back?
discussion.behind: Move toward the doxology and the surrender in it. Everyone clings to one of the three, the control of the kingdom, the strength of the power, the credit of the glory. Help each person name which one they grip, and feel the release of handing it back to the God it always belonged to. The doxology is not flattery of God, it is the return of stolen property.

discussion.q: Bell says we end the prayer smaller than we started, and that this is the only place a human being was ever safe. How is being made smaller by this prayer a rescue rather than a diminishment?
discussion.behind: Close on the reversal and the whole arc of the study. The prayer has been shrinking us and enlarging God from the first word, and the ending completes it. Help the room feel that the smallness is not humiliation but relief, the laying down of a weight we were never meant to carry, the kingdom and power and glory that crushed us when we tried to keep them. End in weight, on the safety of being small before a God this large.

objections.objection: Praying to be delivered from evil and the devil is superstition, a leftover from a pre-scientific age. What people used to call evil we now understand as psychology, trauma, and circumstance. Grown-ups do not believe in a literal devil.
objections.response: Grant the real thing the objection is reacting against, because the church has earned some of this suspicion. Evil has been used as a lazy explanation, a way to avoid the harder work of examining our own hearts and systems, and the cry of devil has too often been aimed at the inconvenient rather than the genuinely wicked, so that a healthy allergy to superstition is understandable. Concede that fully. But watch the confidence of the claim, because it does not survive the historical record. The century that prided itself on outgrowing the category of evil is the same century that produced the death camps, the gulags, the killing fields, industrialized murder on a scale no superstitious age ever managed, and psychology and circumstance, real as they are, do not finally account for it. Something in the honest witness of a survivor, standing before what was done, reaches for a word larger than dysfunction, and the word it reaches for is evil. The petition does not require a cartoon devil with a pitchfork. It requires only the humility to admit that there is a darkness in the world and in us that we did not invent and cannot master alone, and that the mature response to it is not to deny it but to ask to be delivered from it. The prayer is not naive about evil. The confidence that we have outgrown it is.

objections.objection: If I have to ask God not to lead me into temptation, does that mean God is the one tempting me? That makes God the author of my sin, which is monstrous, and the whole petition seems to accuse God of setting me up to fail.
objections.response: This is an old and serious puzzle, and the church has worked on it for centuries rather than waving it away, so it deserves a careful answer. Start where James starts, plainly, that God tempts no one, that he cannot be tempted with evil and does not entice anyone toward it, so whatever the petition means, it cannot mean God is the author of our sin. The key is the Greek word, peirasmos, which means testing and trial as much as it means enticement to evil. Read that way, the petition is not accusing God of luring us but pleading with him about the trials that come, do not let the testing be more than we can bear, do not abandon us to the hour we could not survive, spare us the trial that would break us. It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness and asks not to be brought to the edge of it. The concern was serious enough that in 2019 the Roman Catholic Church approved a revised Italian translation of the line in its liturgy precisely to guard against the misreading that God tempts. God does test, to strengthen and prove his children, but he never entices to evil, and this petition asks the Tester to be also the Deliverer, to keep us in the trial he permits and to rescue us from the evil that would use it against us.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which of the three, the kingdom, the power, or the glory, have you spent your life trying to keep for yourself, and what has the keeping of it cost you?
sessions.practice: This week, pray the whole prayer through, slowly, all the way to the end, and stop on the last line long enough to actually ask, out loud, to be delivered from the specific evil and the specific testing you know is coming this week, naming it rather than praying in general. Then, on the doxology, hand God the one of the three you cling to hardest, the control or the strength or the credit, saying it back to him as his. Write down what it feels like to end the prayer smaller than you began it, and whether the smallness felt like loss or like rest.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. We are weaker than we pretend and the danger is more real than we admit, and we are asking you, honestly, not to let the testing be more than we can bear, and to rescue us from the evil we did not invent and cannot master alone. Keep us in the trials you permit and deliver us from the darkness that would use them against us. And now, at the end, we hand you back what was always yours, the kingdom we tried to keep, the power we thought was ours, the glory we kept taking for ourselves, for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. We end this prayer smaller than we began it, and we have never been so safe. Amen.
reflection: Have I been praying as though I were stronger than I am, or with the honesty that asks not to be brought to the edge of my own weakness?
Where have I explained evil away, in the world or in myself, rather than asking to be delivered from it?
Which of the three, kingdom, power, or glory, do I grip hardest, and what would it mean to hand it back to the God it always belonged to?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the thing that should surprise us most about the Lord's Prayer is how it ends, because it does not end in triumph. We would have ended it in triumph. We would have finished the most important prayer ever taught with a flourish of confidence, a declaration of victory, a strong and rising note. Jesus ends it with a request for rescue. Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. The final petition assumes two things we spend most of our energy denying, that we are weaker than we think, and that the danger around us and inside us is more real than we admit. It is the prayer of a person who has stopped pretending. Now the puzzle, because the church has genuinely struggled with this line and we should not skip the struggle. James, in his letter, says as plainly as it can be said that God tempts no one, that he cannot be tempted with evil and he himself entices no one toward it. So why would Jesus teach us to ask God not to lead us into temptation, as though God were the one doing the tempting. The answer runs partly through the Greek. The word here, peirasmos, means testing and trial every bit as much as it means enticement to sin, and when you hear it that way the petition opens up. It is not accusing God of luring us toward evil. It is a plea about the trials that come to every human life, and the plea is this, do not let the testing be more than we can bear, do not abandon us to the hour we could not survive, spare us, if you will, the trial that would break us. It is the prayer of someone who has taken an honest measure of his own strength and found it wanting, and who asks, humbly, not to be brought to the edge of it. The confusion was serious enough that as recently as 2019 the Roman Catholic Church approved a revision of this line in its liturgy, precisely to keep anyone from hearing it as though God were the author of our temptation. God tests his children to strengthen and prove them. He never entices them to evil. And this petition asks the God who permits the testing to be also the God who delivers through it. Then the second half, deliver us from evil, and here we have to face the modern objection squarely, because it is the reasonable voice in the room. The skeptic says that evil is a primitive category, a leftover from a pre-scientific age, that what our ancestors called the evil one we now understand perfectly well as psychology, trauma, poverty, circumstance, and that grown-ups do not pray to be rescued from a devil. And I want to grant what is true in that, because a great deal is true. Evil has been used as a lazy explanation, a way to avoid the harder and more honest work of examining our own hearts and our own systems. The cry of devil has too often been aimed at the inconvenient person rather than the genuinely wicked deed. A healthy suspicion of superstition is not faithlessness, it is often just honesty. Concede all of it. But now watch the confidence of the claim collapse against the actual record of the age that makes it, because of all the centuries in which to announce that humanity has outgrown the category of evil, the twentieth was the strangest possible choice. That century built the death camps and the gulags and the killing fields. It murdered by the industrial ton, with paperwork, with efficiency, with the full participation of educated and cultured people, and no account made only of psychology and circumstance has ever been able to hold the whole weight of what happened. Stand a survivor in front of it and listen to the word they reach for, because it is almost never dysfunction and almost always evil, a word larger than the machinery, a word for a darkness that exceeds its parts. The petition does not require you to picture a cartoon devil. It requires only the honesty to admit there is a darkness in the world and in you that you did not invent and cannot master by yourself, and that the mature response to it is not to deny it but to ask, daily, to be delivered from it. And now the prayer ends, and the oldest manuscripts of Matthew actually stop at deliver us from evil, but very early, in the ancient document called the Didache from around the turn of the second century, the church was already praying a closing line, and for nearly two thousand years the people of God have ended this prayer the same way. For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen. And I want you to see what that doxology does, because it completes an arc the whole prayer has been tracing from the very first word. The prayer opened by hallowing God's name, making him large, and it has been making him larger and us smaller at every step, praying his kingdom before our bread, his will before our wants, his mercy as the measure of ours, his deliverance because we cannot save ourselves. And now, at the end, it hands him three things by name, and they are precisely the three things we spend our entire lives trying to keep. The kingdom, which is control, the reign we want to be ours. The power, which is strength, the ability we want to be ours. The glory, which is credit, the honor we keep quietly rerouting to ourselves. The prayer takes all three out of our hands and gives them back to the God they always belonged to. And here I have to stand inside it, because I am a man who has tried to keep all three. I have built small kingdoms and called them my life. I have trusted my own power and been ashamed to admit its limits. I have taken glory that was never mine, in a hundred small thefts, wanting the credit, wanting to be seen, wanting the name that is hallowed to share its light with mine. The doxology is where I have to set all of it down. So here is the reversal, the last one, the one the whole prayer was built to reach. We end this prayer smaller than we started it. We began by daring to call God Father, and we end by handing him the kingdom and the power and the glory and keeping nothing back, and every instinct we have says that this is loss, that to be made this small before a God this large is a kind of erasure. It is the opposite. It turns out that the smallness is the safety. It turns out that the weight of the kingdom and the power and the glory was never ours to carry, that we were being crushed by property we had stolen, and that the only place a human being was ever actually safe was here, at the end of this prayer, small, unarmed, emptied of every kingdom but his, saying the last word the prayer gives us to say. Amen. So be it. It is his.

scriptureStudy.note: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. The prayer ends not in confidence but in a plea for protection, confessing our weakness in the testing and our need of rescue from a real evil we cannot overcome alone.

Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God, for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. This governs the reading of the petition, God tests but never entices to sin, so the prayer pleads about the trial and never accuses God of authoring the temptation.

God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will provide the way of escape. Here is the promise beneath the petition, that the faithful God limits the testing and makes a way through, which is exactly what the prayer asks him to do.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation, the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. In Gethsemane Jesus commands the very prayer he taught, tying the petition to the honest admission of our own weakness that makes it necessary.

Simon, Satan demanded to have you, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. Jesus names a real evil that seeks to sift the disciple, and answers it with prayer, the pattern the final petition puts in our own mouths, deliver us from evil.

Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power and the glory, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours, yours is the kingdom, O Lord. David's prayer is the likely root of the doxology, handing God the kingdom, power, and glory that the closing line returns to him.

To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever. The doxology of the prayer anticipates the doxology of heaven, where the whole creation hands God the glory, so the prayer ends by rehearsing on earth what will be sung forever.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the textual and historical history of the ending, because a group is served by honesty about it rather than by pretending the question does not exist. The doxology, for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, is not found in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew, which is why most modern translations place it in a footnote, and a careful group should be told this plainly rather than discovering it later and feeling deceived. But the same honesty reveals something moving, because the doxology is not a late invention at all, it appears in a form already in the Didache, the church's teaching manual from around the turn of the second century, which instructs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, so the church was closing the prayer this way within a generation or two of the apostles, drawing on the ancient words of David's own doxology in First Chronicles. Weigh what it means that the people of God, praying this prayer daily for two thousand years, could not leave it ending on evil and reached for the kingdom and the power and the glory, not to add to Scripture but to answer the darkness of the sixth petition with the sovereignty of God. Set this beside the strong secular refusal of the category of evil, tested against the record, and consider the philosopher Hannah Arendt watching the trial of a Nazi administrator and reaching, famously, for the phrase the banality of evil, an account that names how ordinary and bureaucratic great evil can be while still insisting, against every attempt to reduce it, that it was evil and not mere malfunction. The secular witness gets close to the symptom and cannot finally name the disease or supply the deliverance. Then take up the long tradition of reading the whole prayer as a summary of the Christian life, from Tertullian who called it a summary of the whole gospel, through Augustine who told the widow Proba that whatever else we rightly pray is already contained in these petitions, to the catechisms that expound it line by line. The aim is to end the study where the prayer ends, with the honesty to face a real evil and a real weakness, and the deeper honesty to hand the kingdom, the power, and the glory back to the God to whom they always belonged, which is the only posture in which a human being has ever been safe.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group is a thoughtful skeptic, invited by a friend, and he has been patient through four sessions, but the word evil in the final petition is where he pushes back hardest. He says, honestly and without hostility, that he can appreciate much of this prayer as poetry and wisdom, but that asking to be delivered from evil sounds to him like superstition, and he cannot pretend to believe in a devil. He is not being difficult. He is being honest, and his honesty is a gift to the room. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor his intelligence rather than manage it. Do not rush to defend a cartoon devil, which is not what the petition requires and not what he needs to hear. Grant him what is true, that evil has been used lazily and superstitiously, and that his allergy to it is understandable. Then, without pressing him to believe anything, put the honest question back to him. Ask him whether the century just behind us, with its industrialized murder, is really best described by the word dysfunction, or whether at some point the word evil becomes not a superstition but the only honest name for what happened. Let him sit with it. The aim is not to win the argument tonight but to leave him unable to dismiss the category as naive, thinking, perhaps, that he does not yet believe this prayer, but no longer certain that believing it is stupid. That is a win, and it is the only kind this prayer was ever after with a skeptic.

memoryVerse.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

leaderPrimer: The particular danger of a study on the Lord's Prayer is familiarity. Most people in your room have said these words since childhood, and familiarity does not deepen a thing, it numbs us to it. The first temptation, then, is that everyone arrives certain they already know this prayer, and a room that already knows is a room that cannot be taught. So the work of the first night is to make the familiar strange again, to slow the words down until people hear what they have been reciting on autopilot for years. Do not let the group race ahead to the meaning. Sit in the actual words, one line a week, and trust that the prayer is deep enough to reward the slowness. The second danger is that a study on prayer becomes a study about prayer, a set of ideas discussed and never a single word actually prayed. Refuse that. Every session ends by praying the very line it studied, and if you only do one thing well, pray the prayer with your people rather than merely explaining it to them. There are two places to take special care. The forgiveness session, session four, will land on someone in the room carrying a deep wound, and the petition has been used as a whip against exactly such people. Do not press forgiveness on the wounded. Distinguish it clearly from excusing, from forgetting, and from returning to harm, and where the wound is deep, point toward safety, real help, and patience, never toward a forced and hollow absolution on anyone's timeline but the Spirit's. And the final session names evil plainly, which the skeptic in your room will resist. Honor the resistance. The skeptic is often the most honest person present, and the goal is never to win the argument but to leave him unable to call the faith stupid. Bell leads this from inside it. He came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and is raising five sons, and every one of those facts sits inside this prayer, in the first word he could not feel, in the will he did not want to surrender, in the debts he asked forgiven while withholding forgiveness, in the glory he kept taking. If you present yourself as the master of prayer, the room will perform back at you and nothing will move. Go in as a person still learning to pray the only prayer Jesus taught, still saying words your heart is catching up to. Five weeks will not make anyone a master of prayer. It can make a room hear, for the first time in years, the prayer they have been saying all their lives, and send people home able to pray it awake.

faq.q: Is this study just going to explain a prayer everyone already knows by heart?
faq.a: The opposite. The fact that everyone knows it by heart is the very problem the study is built to address, because familiarity does not deepen a thing, it numbs us to it, and most people have recited the Lord's Prayer for so long they no longer hear a single word of it. The study slows the prayer down to one line a week, so that words worn smooth by repetition become sharp again. It takes the scandal of calling God Father, the cost of praying your will be done, the honesty of asking for bread, the terror of the word as in forgive us as we forgive, and the humility of asking to be delivered from evil, and it treats each as though you were hearing it for the first time. The goal is not to teach a prayer you already know but to help you finally pray the one you have been saying on autopilot for years.

faq.q: Do I need to know a lot about the Bible or theology to lead or join this study?
faq.a: No. The study was built to be led by an ordinary person with no preparation and joined by anyone, including someone who has never prayed a serious prayer in their life. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends by simply praying the line it studied. It handles the harder questions, the puzzle about whether God tempts us, the debate over what daily bread means, the tension in forgive us as we forgive, but it handles them plainly and never requires you to have studied them beforehand. If you can read the prayer slowly and be honest about your own struggle to pray it, you can lead this, and if you have only ever said these words without thinking, you are exactly who it was written for.

faq.q: Why does the study spend so much time on the word as in forgive us as we forgive?
faq.a: Because it is the most terrifying word in the prayer and the one we most reliably skip. Jesus did not say forgive us because we forgive, as though we earned it, and he did not say so that we can forgive, as though ours came second. He said as, in the same measure we are handing out, and then he reinforced it the moment the prayer ended, saying that if we do not forgive others, neither will our Father forgive us. The study faces this squarely, refusing both the reading that makes forgiveness a wage we earn, which would shatter grace, and the reading that softens the word until it means nothing, which has to delete the plainest words Jesus spoke. The point is not that our forgiving purchases God's, but that a person who has truly received an ocean of mercy and then withholds a teaspoon of it has proven he never understood what he received. The forgiven forgive.

faq.q: Session four talks about forgiveness. What if I have been deeply wounded and cannot just forgive?
faq.a: The study takes this with complete seriousness and refuses the cruelty that has been done in this petition's name. Forgiveness has been used as a whip against the wounded, telling the betrayed and the abused that their healing depends on excusing what was done to them, and the study says plainly that this is a misuse the prayer never sponsored. Forgiveness is not saying the wrong was not wrong. It is not excusing, not forgetting, not pretending, and it is never returning to the reach of someone still doing harm. It is the eventual release of your right to make the person pay, worked slowly by the Spirit for your own freedom, and it does not require reconciliation with an unrepentant or dangerous person. There is no timeline you owe anyone. Where the wound is deep, the study points toward safety, real help, and patience, and it insists the God of this prayer is on the side of the wounded, never asking anyone to call a wound acceptable in order to be free of it.

faq.q: Does the study really say God might lead me into temptation? That sounds like it blames God for my sin.
faq.a: It faces that exact puzzle head on rather than dodging it. James says plainly that God tempts no one and cannot be tempted with evil, so whatever the petition means, it cannot mean God is the author of our sin. The key is the Greek word, peirasmos, which means testing and trial as much as enticement to evil, so the petition is best heard as a plea, do not let the testing be more than we can bear, do not abandon us to the trial, spare us the hour we could not survive. God does test his children to strengthen them, but he never entices them toward evil. The concern was serious enough that the Roman Catholic Church revised the wording of the line in its liturgy in 2019 precisely to guard against the misreading. So the petition does not accuse God, it asks the God who permits the testing to be also the one who delivers us through it.

faq.q: Is the ending, for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, actually in the Bible?
faq.a: The study is honest about this rather than hiding it. The doxology is not found in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew, which is why most modern translations place it in a footnote, and you deserve to know that plainly. But the same honesty reveals something moving, because the closing is not a late invention. It appears in a form already in the Didache, the church's teaching manual from around the turn of the second century, drawing on the ancient words of David's own doxology in First Chronicles, so the church was ending the prayer this way within a generation or two of the apostles. The people of God, praying this prayer daily for two thousand years, could not leave it ending on the word evil and reached for the kingdom and the power and the glory, not to add to Scripture but to answer the darkness of the last petition with the sovereignty of God.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not this just religion teaching people to recite words and feel spiritual?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study earns the right to answer it by refusing exactly that move. It does not treat the prayer as a formula that works spiritual magic, and Jesus himself warned against heaping up empty phrases the way the pagans do. What the study offers instead is a slow, honest reading of a prayer that, examined closely, does the opposite of flattering the one who prays it. It spends four of its six petitions on God before it ever mentions your needs. It asks you to surrender your own will, to depend for your bread, to forgive as you would be forgiven, to admit you are weaker than you think and the evil is more real than you say. This is not a prayer that tells you what you wanted to hear. You do not have to believe it to notice that it is stranger and more demanding than the religion you were expecting, and to wonder what kind of person could have composed a prayer built entirely to make the one saying it smaller and God larger.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the writer instead of just teaching the prayer?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is the message. The writer came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and is raising five sons, and he does not stand outside the struggles this prayer exposes. He prayed the word Father for years before he could feel it meant anything. He built small kingdoms and prayed your will be done while making sure his own was done. He asked God for forgiveness in the same breath he withheld it from someone else. He took the glory that belonged to God in a hundred small thefts. He writes from inside the prayer, not from above it, and the study asks every leader and every person to do the same, because you cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue, and you cannot teach people to pray from a height without turning the teaching into performance. A study that pointed only at other people's failures to pray would let everyone off the hook and change no one. By keeping the writer inside the prayer, it makes honest prayer possible for the people actually in the room.

faq.q: How is this study structured, and how long does it take?
faq.a: It is five sessions, one for each movement of the prayer, and it can be run as five weeks straight, as seven weeks with the harder sessions given two weeks each, or as a four-week intensive that pairs the opening sessions. Session one takes the address and the reverence, Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Session two takes the two petitions that pray against our own preferences, your kingdom come, your will be done. Session three takes the request for daily bread, dependence and enough. Session four takes the terrifying conjunction, forgive us as we forgive. Session five takes the final petition and the doxology, lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, and the kingdom, the power, and the glory. Each session runs about fifty minutes, opening briefly, discussing for the bulk of the time, and closing by praying the line it studied. No homework is required, though a weekly practice is offered for those who want to carry the prayer into their week.

faq.q: What makes this different from any other book or study on the Lord's Prayer?
faq.a: Two things. First, it refuses to turn the prayer into a technique for getting what you want from God, which is where most popular teaching on prayer quietly ends up. This prayer spends four of its six petitions before it ever mentions your bread, and the whole thing is built to make you smaller and God larger, which is the opposite of what we came to prayer hoping to arrange, and the study honors that shape instead of fighting it. Second, it does not soften the hard parts. It sits in the terror of the word as, faces the puzzle about God and temptation, tells the honest truth about the doxology and the manuscripts, and names evil plainly in a skeptical age. It writes toward the doubter and the wounded as much as toward the settled believer, granting the strongest objections their full weight before it answers them, and it ends not in a tidy resolution but in the weight of a prayer that hands God everything.

faq.q: Can this study help someone who does not really know how to pray at all?
faq.a: That is precisely who it was written for. The disciples who first heard this prayer did not know how to pray either, which is why they asked Jesus to teach them, and his answer was not a technique or a mood but words, pray like this, a trellis for a faith not yet strong enough to stand on its own. The study takes that seriously. It does not assume you arrive knowing how to pray, and it does not try to manufacture a feeling. It gives you the words Jesus gave, one line at a time, and helps you grow into them, so that the memorized prayer becomes the training of real prayer rather than the enemy of it. If you have never known where to begin, you begin here, with the only prayer Jesus ever taught, and you let the words wait, faithfully, for your heart to catch up.

faq.q: Does taking this prayer seriously mean the study looks down on people who struggle to pray or whose minds wander?
faq.a: No, and it is careful here. The writer is candid that he prayed the word Father for years before he could feel it, and that his mind wandered to his calendar while his mouth said the words, so the wandering mind is not treated as a disqualification but as the ordinary condition of praying people. The study distinguishes honestly between the gap that is hypocrisy and the gap that is faith reaching past the feeling, the way a wound heals before it feels healed. Jesus gave his friends words precisely because they could not yet compose their own, and the study honors that, treating the struggle to pray not as a failure to be ashamed of but as the very reason the prayer was given. The point is never to make anyone feel they pray badly. It is to help everyone, the struggler most of all, finally hear the prayer they have been saying.

timeline.event: Jesus teaches the prayer to his disciples, both in the Sermon on the Mount recorded in Matthew and, in Luke, in direct answer to the request, Lord, teach us to pray, giving his followers not a technique but words to grow into.

In Gethsemane, Jesus prays the heart of the prayer for real, saying Abba, Father, and not my will but yours be done, showing that the surrender of your will be done is trust brought through honest desire, not resignation.

Paul writes that the Spirit of adoption places the very word Jesus used, Abba, Father, in the mouths of believers, so that the intimacy of the Son's own address to the Father becomes the shared possession of the adopted.

The Didache, the earliest Christian teaching manual, instructs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day and already includes a form of the closing doxology, showing the church prayed this prayer daily within a generation of the apostles.

Tertullian writes his treatise On Prayer, calling the Lord's Prayer a summary of the whole gospel, the first of many patristic commentaries that treat the prayer as the pattern of the entire Christian life.

Cyprian of Carthage writes On the Lord's Prayer, dwelling on the audacity of calling God Father and on the plural of the petitions, insisting the Christian never prays for himself alone but always as part of the whole body.

Origen writes his treatise On Prayer, noting that the word translated daily, epiousios, appears almost nowhere else in Greek and seems to have been coined for this prayer, a puzzle scholars have weighed ever since.

Augustine, writing his letter to the widow Proba on prayer, teaches that whatever else we rightly pray is already contained within the petitions of the Lord's Prayer, so that it is the measure and the summary of all true prayer.

Martin Luther writes A Simple Way to Pray for his barber, Peter, teaching him to pray by walking slowly through the Lord's Prayer petition by petition, using the ancient words as the living trellis for personal prayer.

John Calvin, in the final edition of his Institutes, devotes the fullest part of his treatment of prayer to expounding the Lord's Prayer line by line, answering the objection that prayer is pointless if God is sovereign.

The Westminster Assembly, in the Shorter Catechism, expounds the Lord's Prayer petition by petition as the model of all prayer, a pattern the Heidelberg Catechism had already followed, teaching generations to pray it with understanding.

The Roman Catholic Church approves a revised wording of the line lead us not into temptation in its liturgy, to guard against the misreading that God is the author of our temptation, reflecting a debate as old as the petition itself.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. We are going to do something strange with a prayer most of us have known since we were children, which is to actually slow it down and hear it. Before we start, three things. First, familiarity is our enemy tonight, so the goal is not to prove we already know this prayer but to hear it as if for the first time, and there are no wrong answers in the first few minutes, only honest ones. Second, we are not here to perform. You can be unsure, you can admit your mind wanders when you pray, you can say you have said these words for years without meaning them, and that honesty is exactly where we start, and what is said here stays here. Third, the writer puts himself inside every line of this prayer. He came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and is raising five sons, and he is still learning to pray this. So are we. One more thing that matters. If this study touches a real wound, especially the session on forgiveness, you are not required to resolve it on anyone's schedule, and I am available to talk privately and to point toward real help. Tonight we are sitting with this line: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will simply sit with it before we say anything at all.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what this line says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the actual prayers each of us prays or fails to pray, because none of this matters if it stays an idea about prayer in general instead of the prayer you will try to say this week.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it does not tie up neatly, because a prayer is not a problem solved in an evening and the writer does not resolve it for us either. Take the weight of this line home with you. Try the practice this week, in your own prayers, even badly. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And now, before we go, we are going to do the one thing this whole study is finally about. We are going to pray the line we just studied, together, slowly, and mean it as best we can. Then I will see you next time. Thank you for the honesty it took to be here, and my door is open if any of you needs it.

cadences.name: The full study (7 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rule that familiarity is the enemy, and pray the whole prayer through slowly once, hearing it before studying it.
Week 2: Session 1, Our Father in Heaven, Hallowed Be Your Name, the address and the reverence held together.
Week 3: Session 2, Your Kingdom Come, Your Will Be Done, with extended time on Gethsemane and praying against our own preferences.
Week 4: Session 3, Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread, dependence, the manna, and the freedom of enough.
Week 5: Session 4, Forgive Us Our Debts, As We Forgive, with careful time on the word as and private space for the wounded.
Week 6: Session 5, Lead Us Not Into Temptation, But Deliver Us From Evil, the final petition and the doxology.
Week 7: Integration. Pray the whole prayer through together line by line, revisit the practices, and close on the kingdom, the power, and the glory handed back to God.

bibliography.title: Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: The pastoral spine of the study, where Keller holds together the awe and the intimacy the first session insists on and treats the Lord's Prayer as the school of Christian prayer. Anchors sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Lord and His Prayer
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: A short and rich set of meditations walking through the prayer petition by petition, reading it within the story of Jesus and the kingdom. Supports every session, especially the kingdom material of session 2. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them.

bibliography.title: Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's informal letters on the life of prayer, honest about the wandering mind and the strangeness of asking, useful background for the honesty this study asks of leaders and groups. Background for sessions 1 and 3. Not cited directly.

bibliography.title: On the Lord's Prayer
bibliography.author: Cyprian of Carthage
bibliography.note: The third-century treatise dwelling on the audacity of calling God Father and on the plural of the petitions, that the Christian never prays alone. Historical anchor for sessions 1 and 3. Leader to handle as a tradition's reading.

bibliography.title: On Prayer
bibliography.author: Origen of Alexandria
bibliography.note: The third-century treatise that first noted the rare word epiousios and reflected deeply on the whole prayer. Cited in the study for the daily bread material of session 3. Leader to confirm before pressing any specific argument as the study's own.

bibliography.title: A Simple Way to Pray
bibliography.author: Martin Luther
bibliography.note: Luther's letter to his barber, teaching prayer by walking slowly through the Lord's Prayer petition by petition, the model for using the ancient words as a living trellis. Supports the study's method throughout. Historical background for the timeline.

bibliography.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, Chapter 20
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: Calvin's fullest treatment of prayer, expounding the Lord's Prayer line by line and answering the objection that prayer is pointless under God's sovereignty. Essential for the sovereignty question in session 2. Leader to weigh carefully.

bibliography.title: Waiting for God
bibliography.author: Simone Weil
bibliography.note: Includes a searching meditation on the Our Father, attentive to the reordering of the self the prayer works. A demanding and unconventional voice, offered as a witness rather than a settled guide. Background for sessions 2 and 5. Leader to weigh with discernment.

bibliography.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
bibliography.author: Hannah Arendt
bibliography.note: The secular account that names how ordinary great evil can be while refusing to reduce it to mere malfunction, cited in session 5 against the claim that evil is a naive category. Common grace, true as far as it goes and unable to supply the deliverance.

bibliography.title: The Prayers of Jesus
bibliography.author: Joachim Jeremias
bibliography.note: The mid-twentieth-century study that recovered the intimacy of the word Abba, cited in session 1. To be read alongside its careful correction rather than on its own, since the popular overreach it inspired has been rightly qualified.

bibliography.title: Abba Isn't Daddy (Journal of Theological Studies essay)
bibliography.author: James Barr
bibliography.note: The 1988 essay correcting the popular claim that Abba simply means Daddy, cited in session 1 to keep the intimacy of the address real without making it cheap or childish. Essential balance for the Abba material.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of Matthew
bibliography.author: the Evangelist Matthew
bibliography.note: The primary text, chapter six, where the prayer is given within the Sermon on the Mount, to be read and prayed and not only cited. The book at the heart of the whole study.

furtherReading: Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God, Timothy Keller, for those who want the fuller pastoral case behind holding awe and intimacy together as sessions 1 and 5 do.
The Lord and His Prayer, N. T. Wright, for readers who want a short, warm walk through the prayer within the story of the kingdom, leader to confirm specific claims.
A Simple Way to Pray, Martin Luther, for anyone who wants to practice the study's method, praying the prayer slowly line by line as a trellis for their own words.
Institutes, Book 3, Chapter 20, John Calvin, for those willing to sit with the deep question of session 2, how prayer and God's sovereignty hold together.
The Gospel of Matthew, chapters five through seven, read straight through, for those who want to hear the prayer in the setting Jesus gave it, inside the Sermon on the Mount.

glossary.definition: The Aramaic word for father that Jesus used in Gethsemane and handed to his disciples, a word of family intimacy. Real and profound without being a nursery word, as the debate between Jeremias and James Barr clarified, and now placed in the believer's mouth by the Spirit of adoption.

Made holy, set apart, treated as sacred. To pray hallowed be your name is to ask that God's name be known and honored as holy, and to align the one praying with God's own deepest purpose before asking anything for oneself.

The reign of God breaking into the world, prayed to come in the present tense. Not a passive acceptance of the way things are but an active overturning, feeding the hungry, healing the broken, casting down the mighty, which is why praying your kingdom come makes a person restless for justice.

The daily surrender of our own way to God's, modeled in Gethsemane, where the honest desire is named fully and then laid down. Surrender, which is trust, not resignation, which is mere defeat, and the difference between them is everything.

The rare Greek word translated daily in give us this day our daily bread, so uncommon that Origen thought it coined for this prayer. However its exact sense is settled, it points to bread for the day rather than for the storehouse, training a daily dependence.

The ordinary provision the prayer asks for, one day at a time, teaching that we did not make ourselves and cannot keep ourselves. A confession of dependence and a discipline of enough, prayed in the plural, Give us, which enlists the one praying in the feeding of the hungry.

The small conjunction in forgive us as we forgive, the most terrifying word in the prayer. Not because we earn forgiveness, but because withholding it proves we never received it. The measure of mercy we hand out is the measure we are asking God to use.

The Greek word in lead us not into temptation, meaning testing and trial as much as enticement to evil. Read this way the petition pleads, do not let the testing be more than we can bear, and never accuses God, who tests his children but tempts no one.

The plea for rescue that ends the prayer proper, confessing a real evil in the world and in us that we did not invent and cannot master alone. Not a cartoon devil but the darkness the twentieth century made it impossible to call naive.

The closing line, for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever, absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew but present in the Didache within a generation, drawn from David's prayer in First Chronicles. The church's refusal to end the prayer on the word evil.

The distinction at the heart of your will be done. Resignation is the shrug of the defeated who gives up because nothing can be done. Surrender is the act of the trusting who lays down what they wanted into hands they believe are good.

The prayer's deliberate order, spending four of its six petitions on God's name, kingdom, and will before it mentions our bread, so that the whole thing makes the one praying smaller and God larger, which is the opposite of prayer as a technique for getting what we want.

The earliest Christian teaching manual, from around the turn of the second century, which instructs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day and already includes a form of the doxology, evidence of how early and how daily the church prayed this prayer.
